vignette:
Bao, a 47-year-old park ranger, speaks in a low, measured tone, as if conserving energy. Eight months have passed since his daughter, Mai, recovered, but the relief he expected never arrived. Instead, a quiet but persistent storm took its place. It began on a Tuesday afternoon when he found his ten-year-old daughter, usually vibrant and full of life, lying listless on the sofa with a raging fever. A wave of dizziness washed over him as he scooped her into his arms, a disorienting lurch of terror that he now recognizes as the first tremor. At the urgent care clinic, a dismissive doctor, whose breath carried the faint, sharp scent of alcohol-based hand sanitizer, diagnosed a bad flu and sent them home. Bao argued, pointing to Mai's frightening lethargy, but the doctor waved him off. Hours later, Mai had a seizure, and the world dissolved into the shriek of an ambulance siren and the sterile, pervasive smell of the hospital's emergency department. She was diagnosed with a severe case of bacterial meningitis; the doctors said another hour would have been too late.

Mai is healthy now, racing around the park visitor center after school just as she used to. But Bao remains trapped in the hours of the crisis. He spends long stretches of his day, often while walking familiar trails at work, consumed by thoughts of the first doctor. He replays the consultation endlessly, imagining all the things he should have said, the demands he should have made. These thoughts curdle into elaborate fantasies of revenge: a meticulously crafted complaint to the medical board, a lawsuit that would strip the man of his license, a public confrontation that would expose his incompetence to the world. He finds himself dwelling on this injustice, a bitter preoccupation that has become the central organizing principle of his thoughts. At home, this internal focus has built a wall between him and his wife. When she tries to talk about their shared ordeal, to process the fear they both felt, Bao feels a surge of agitation and leaves the room. He cannot bear to be reminded of it by her, to hear the story from another person's mouth. It is his burden to carry, his fight to wage internally. This strategy of internal containment has had the paradoxical effect of making the external world feel more threatening, priming him to notice any sensory detail that echoes the crisis.

Certain sensory experiences have become fraught with a danger he cannot articulate. At the park's small first-aid station, the simple act of a colleague tearing open an antiseptic wipe can make his breath catch in his throat. Last month, while helping a park visitor who had fallen, the smell of beer on the man's breath was so overwhelming that Bao had to step away, feigning the need to retrieve something from his truck. Sometimes, when rising too quickly from a crouch to inspect a trail marker, he is ambushed by a sudden, intense lightheadedness that brings a cold sweat to his skin.

These separate currents of his experience-the internal, churning anger and the external, sensory threats-have left him feeling estranged from his own life. The joy he should feel watching his daughter thrive is muted, held at a distance by the constant, low-grade hum of resentment. His wife, patient for months, finally told him she felt like she was living with a ghost, one who was furious at a world that had already moved on. It was this fear-not of the past, but of losing the family he had fought so hard to save-that finally brought Bao to seek help. He wants to be present again, to stand in the sunlit clearing of his life without constantly scanning the tree line for a threat he can neither fight nor flee.
